newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Pacific island states attack Australian report.
newsitem.headline: Pacific island states attack Australian report.

text.p: An embarrassed Australian government scrambled on Saturday to limit the diplomatic damage from the publication of a highly critical secret report on its South Pacific neighbours.
The tiny South Pacific island state of Nauru said the government report criticising Nauru and other island states for mismanagement and corruption was an insulting "gossip column".

The Cook Islands said the report was offensive and contained "significant inaccuracies", Australia's opposition labelled the report a major diplomatic blunder and the influential Democrats party condemned it as "incompetent and unprofessional".

In damage control, Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer on Saturday tried to distance the government from the report, assuring offended South Pacific nations it was not government policy.
"Such briefing material is not of itself government policy nor an expression of the government's views," Downer said in a statement.
"I have instructed Australian Heads of Mission in the South Pacific to convey these views to their host governments as soon as possible," Downer said.

The paper was prepared jointly by the foreign ministry and treasury for Treasurer Peter Costello as a briefing for last weekend's summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum in the tropical resort town of Cairns.
It was left on a table in a public area at the summit where it was obtained by Reuters.
The document warned of impending economic disaster in several island countries, citing mismanagement and corruption and detailing the personal habits of political leaders.
The 93-page document marked 'AUSTEO', or Australian Eyes Only, said Nauru was on the brink of calamity and in such bad shape it might lose its independence.

Nauru President Kinza Clodumar said in a statement that the document was "most insulting and patronising" to the Nauru government. "I am sure they are feeling very hurt -- it's a most dreadful report," Clodumar said.
"As reported, the document sounded as though it was heavily laced with rumour and scuttlebutt, rather than an attempt to provide sound analytical advice," he said.
Clodumar said that despite being "so badly and inaccurately advised by their officials", he believed the Australian ministers at Cairns "paid little attention to the gossip column".

Cook Island Prime Minister Sir Geoffrey Henry was upset by the report, which contained "significant inaccuracies", the prime minister's deputy chief of staff told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio.
Among the dry statistics on economic growth, debt service levels and budget deficits, the paper also provided Costello with tidbits about the personal behaviour of some of his guests.

It described what it said were the drinking habits of some island ministers, including whether they became belligerent or mellow when drunk, along with personal traits, family crises and religious habits.
Some were labelled corrupt -- one was nicknamed "Mister Ten Percent", another was "corrupt, spurns due process and advice and attracts carpetbaggers". Others were portrayed simply as incompetent.
Australia's acting Labor opposition leader Gareth Evans said: "In one instance we have offended 15 countries".
"I cannot recall a document as systematically offensive ever being written while I was foreign minister," he said.
"It's crucially important that there be a public apology. Some real humble pie will have to be eaten by Mr Costello...he's going to find it embarrassing but it's the least Australia can do."
Australian Democrats leader Cheryl Kernot also condemned the document. "This is very damaging, it's an example of gross incompetence and unprofessionalism," Kernot said.

Australia and New Zealand are the forum's biggest economies, dwarfing the poorer island nations -- the Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Nauru, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Palau, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.
Most South Pacific economies are afflicted by low growth, high debt, bloated public sectors, growing populations and weak or virtually non-existent private sectors.
